title: Vendi Anomaly Scores for Efficient and Accurate Anomaly Detection
claim: Removing an anomalous sample shifts the dataset's spectrum far more than removing a normal one, making the resulting score separate the two groups.
layout: 3 panels: scatter left, two stacked bar plots top-right, histogram bottom-right; color-coded
description: The left panel is a 2-D scatter plot titled 'Contaminated Dataset'. It shows a large blue cluster of normal points and a smaller red group of anomalies on the right. One normal point and one anomaly are circled in black. On the right, two stacked bar charts share an 'Eigenvalue index' axis from 1 to 32 and plot the change in each eigenvalue. The top chart, 'Effect of Removing Normal Sample', has tiny teal bars, a 'SMALL SPECTRAL IMPACT' label and 'Vendi Score Increase: +0.5%'. The bottom chart, 'Effect of Removing Anomaly', has large red bars, a 'LARGE SPECTRAL IMPACT' label and 'Vendi Score Decrease: 1.2%'. Below them, a histogram with density curves shows the Vendi score after removing a sample. The red anomaly distribution sits on the left, the blue normal distribution on the right, and a dashed vertical line separates them. Blue and red encode normal and anomalous samples throughout.
caption: Overview of VAS. Left: A multimodal dataset contaminated with an anomaly. Right: Removing a rare anomalous point induces a larger change in the eigenvalue spectrum than removing a normal sample. VAS detects these shifts by estimating the change in Vendi Score, derived from the Rényi entropy of order q of the spectrum (Eq. 1).
abstract: Anomaly detection (AD) is a critical for trustworthy machine learning and scientific discovery. Existing methods typically define anomalies through local density, isolation heuristics, or distance from a fitted distribution, making them sensitive to neighborhood scale, partitioning choices, or restrictive distributional assumptions. In this work, we introduce a new paradigm by formulating anomaly detection from a diversity perspective. We propose the $\textit{Vendi Anomaly Score}$ (VAS), which detects anomalies by quantifying how much a sample changes the diversity of the dataset, as measured by the Vendi score, when removed. VAS captures both local redundancy and global data structure without relying on density estimation or partitioning heuristics. Moreover, VAS requires no hyperparameter tuning, instead adapting automatically to the spectral structure of the data. VAS is non-parametric and scales linearly with dataset size. Across 148 benchmark embedding datasets derived from 10 source datasets and 4 embedding architectures, VAS achieves state-of-the-art AD performance. We further validate VAS on large-scale ImageNet experiments, where it remains robust as both contamination rate and dataset scale increase.
